TitleC: Giant Tunability of Intersubband Transitions and Quantum Hall Quartets in Ultrathin InSe
AbstractC: We demonstrate population and characterization of the second subband in few-layer InSe quantum wells, and observation of giant tunability of the intersubband transitions via control of layer thickness and out-of-plane electric field. At high magnetic fields, the simultaneous occupation of two subbands, together with the spin degrees of freedom, leads to the formation of electronic quartets in the quantum Hall regime, where the ring-shaped crossings of Landau levels between the two subbands reveal a series of quantum phase transitions between paramagnetic and ferromagnetic states.

AbstractA: This talk will present my (biased!) perspective of what two-dimensional (2D) materials could be good for. For example, they could be good for applications where their ultrathin nature gives them distinct advantages, such as flexible electronics [1] or light-weight solar cells [2]. They may not be good where conventional materials work sufficiently well, like transistors thicker than a few nanometers. I will focus on 2D materials for 3D heterogeneous integration of electronics, which presents major advantages for energy-efficient computing [3]. Here, 2D materials could be monolayer transistors with ultralow leakage [4] (due to larger band gaps than silicon), used to access high-density memory [5]. Recent results from our group [6,7] and others [8] have shown monolayer transistors with good performance, which cannot be achieved with sub-nanometer thin conventional semiconductors, and the 2D performance could be further boosted by strain [9]. I will also describe some unconventional applications, using 2D materials as thermal insulators [10], heat spreaders [11], and thermal transistors [12]. These could enable control of heat in “thermal circuits” analogous with electrical circuits. Combined, these studies reveal fundamental limits and some unusual applications of 2D materials, which take advantage of their unique properties.  Refs: [1] A. Daus et al., Nat. Elec. 4, 495 (2021). AbstractB:
A large portion of research in 2D materials is limited to mechanical exfoliation of van der Waals (vdW) materials. Chemical exfoliation is a relatively under-utilized route for preparing ultra-thin quantum materials, but it accesses 2D materials that cannot be obtained by mechanical “Scotch -taping.'” It is also a way to mass produce 2D materials, as mechanical taping only accesses small amounts, insufficient for industrial applications. However, chemical exfoliation comes with the drawback that it commonly introduces many defects into the 2D sheets. In this talk I will show the challenges of using chemical exfoliation for 2D quantum materials synthesis, to then introduce two systems in which the approach was successful.
I will show that we can use chemical exfoliation to synthesize large qualities of stable and magnetic monolayers of VOCl. Films of these high-quality sheets are shown to possess similar magnetic properties as the bulk crystals. I will also discuss the synthesis of a stable, aqueous ink of superconducting 1T'-WS2 monolayers. Films printed with the ink are superconducting below 7.3 K and show typical behavior of 2D superconductivity. This ink and its dried, printed version, is stable in ambient conditions. It is ideally suited for applications in flexible and printed electronics. Thus, we were able to establish that chemical exfoliation is of use for quantum materials synthesis.
TitleD: Controlled CVD growth of multilayer hBN for 2.5D applications
AbstractD:
Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is an essential material for 2D materials research and applications. We have developed the CVD growth of multilayer hBN to be used as a 2D insulator. We found that Fe-Ni alloy gives relatively uniform multilayer hBN and the hBN can strongly enhance the PL from WS2 [1]. The unique crystallographic change of the Fe-Ni thin film during the hBN growth was revealed [2]. More recently, we demonstrated the CVD growth and transfer of uniform and large-area multilayer hBN, which significantly increases the carrier mobility of monolayer graphene [3].
I will also introduce our new group research project, “Science of 2.5 Dimensional Materials: Paradigm Shift of Materials Science Toward Future Social Innovation” supported by Ministry of Education, Science and Technology (MEXT), Japan that started from September 2021 [4,5].

TitleA: Industrial Development and Challenges of 2D Electronics for Next Generation CMOS Logic Applications
AbstractA: In recent years, two-dimensional (2D) materials have garnered significant attention as promising candidates for the next generation of electronic devices. In particular, 2D transition metal chalcogenides (TMDs) have emerged as attractive materials for fabricating high-performance field-effect transistors (FETs). At Samsung, we have been actively working on the development of 2D FETs, including multi-bridge channel FETs (MBCFETs). In this talk, I will present our latest findings on the fabrication and development of 2D MBCFETs. I will highlight the unique characteristics of these devices and their potential for use in advanced logic circuits. In addition, I will discuss the challenges we face in scaling up the production of these devices and our ongoing efforts to overcome these challenges. The talk will also provide a glimpse into the future of 2D FETs at Samsung and our vision for the role they will play in shaping the next generation of electronic devices.

TitleC: Symmetry engineering and subband electronics using van der Waals assmbly of transition metal dichalcogenides
AbstractC:
First, we demonstrate that the spatial inversion symmetry and hence the spin splitting in band structure can be controlled by van der Waals assembly with a controlled twist angle. Twisted bilayer WTe2 with twist angle θtwist = 0° and 180° are investigated. The intensity of second harmonic generation changes by two orders of magnitude depending on θtwist, indicating that 1L WTe2 +1L WTe2 (0°) possesses the spatial inversion symmetry, whereas 1L WTe2 +1L WTe2 (180°) lacks the inversion symmetry. The electronic structure of the 1L WTe2 +1L WTe2 are significantly modulated by θtwist. The spin splitting emerges when θtwist = 180° as a consequence of the broken inversion symmetry. The effect induced by controlling the symmetry is quite robust with respect to θtwist fluctuation and inhomogeneity, suggesting the feasibility of pursuing new physical phenomena in 2D materials based on symmetry engineering.
   Next, we study subband quantum states in multi-layer WSe2 for future subband electronics and optoelectronics. Multi-layer transition metal dichalcogenides have been found to exhibit discrete subbands, called van der Waals quantum well (vdW-QW) states. Using momentum-conserved resonant tunneling, we investigate the vdW-QW states in 3L-WSe2/h-BN/3L-WSe2 tunnel junctions with twist angles θtunnel. Current–voltage characteristics exhibit multiple resonant tunneling peaks whose positions shift as θtunnel was varied over the 0–60° range. These results were in good agreement with calculated angular dispersion in conduction band in 3L-WSe2, which indicated the presence of a spin-polarized subband crossing and a saddle point. Our twist-controlled resonant tunneling approach overcomes the difficulties associated with momentum-resolved electronic structure measurements and reveals the unique vdW-QW states in the conduction band of multi-layer WSe2.
TitleD: Unconventional vdW Heterostructures from Bespoke 2D Atomic and Molecular Lattices
AbstractD: Quantum materials have the potential to revolutionize sensing, analytical instrumentation, information processing, and energy conversion. Unconventional vdW superlattices assembled from precisely tailored 2D atomic and molecular lattices encode heterointerfaces which can provide an unprecedented control over charge, exciton, and spin states leading to unique artificial quantum solids. Realizing such superlattices requires not only rational, mechanism-driven chemical synthesis of atomically-precise 2D crystals, but also careful optical spectroscopy and device studies for rigorous determination of fundamental properties and intrinsic limits. In this talk I will review our key prior achievements and emerging results towards the assembly of these unconventional superlattices. First, we show that innovative surface-treatments and precursor chemistries can dramatically alter the dimensionality, morphology, and defect level of 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMD) grown by chemical vapor deposition (CVD). Second, we demonstrate the promise of gas-phase methods for the synthesis of single monolayer 2D molecular lattices (e.g., metal-organic frameworks), and also demonstrate their response to chemical, optical, and electrical stimuli through device transport and scanning probe measurements. Finally, we show that the merger, through direct CVD deposition or exfoliation and transfer, of these 2D crystals yields unique heterointerfaces that can elicit photon upconversion, modulation of lattice phonons, and control of exciton dynamics. Ultimately, the unprecedented array of chemical, dielectric, and mechanical potentials that such superlattices can support open unique opportunities for breakthroughs in optics, sensing, information processing, and sustainability.

TitleA: Symmetry engineering and bulk photovoltaic effect in TMD nanomaterials
AbstractA:
A noticeable advantage of nanomaterials including 2D materials and nanotubes is that their structural symmetry can be changed by forming nanostructures, i.e., isolating monolayers or making van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures, even though we use chemically identical materials. This is in marked contrast with bulk single crystals, where the structural symmetry is uniquely defined by their space group. In this presentation, we discuss the bulk photovoltaic effect (BPVE) on three nanomaterials, based on transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD). BPVE means the photovoltaic effect or zero-bias photocurrent without p-n junctions. BPVE effect is a unique property of noncentrosymmetric materials, and it is the second order nonlinear phenomenon in terms of the electric field of light. 
We have so far reported three examples, TMD nanotube [1], vdW heterostructure [2], and strained TMDs [3]. Through these works, we found that BPVE of H-type monolayer TMDs with trigonal symmetry, such as MoS2 and WS2, is less than the detection limit, despite that the trigonal symmetry allows BPVE. However, it was realized that large BPVE emerges once its symmetry is further reduced by making tublar structures or vdW heterostuctures. All these results indicate that the symmetry reduction from nonpolar trigonal to polar structure plays crucial roles in the bulk photovoltaic effects in TMD nanomaterials. Very interestingly, the BPVE coefficients of the three systems are comparable, an understanding of which will enrich our knowledge concerning the microscopic mechanism of the BPVE in non-centrosymmetric systems, and toward the application of this phenomenon.

TitleA: Inorganic Liquid Crystals Based On 2D Materials
AbstractA: Liquid crystals (LCs) provide tunable birefringence via external stimuli. LC based optical modulators have been widely used in displays, smart windows and other related fields. Conventional organic LCs are suffering from the instable operation under UV exposure and extremely low magneto-optic coefficient. In this talk, I will present our recent discovery of a new type of LCs based on inorganic 2D materials. Due to the close interplay among anisotropies in magnetism, optics and shape, we observed a giant magneto-optic Cotton-Mouton coefficient in a magnetic 2D material with a wide bandgap [1]. Its coefficient is three orders of magnitude larger than that of all reported transparent birefringent media. With the development of a solvent-only size-sorting method [2], we found a quadratic dependence of the magneto-optic coefficient with the lateral size of 2D materials. Such a large coefficient can be further doubled by introducing the collective behavior into the colloidal system of 2D materials [3]. The large magneto-optic coefficient and wide transmission windows cooperatively enable the first observation of transmissive magneto-colouration effect as well as the first fabrication of see-through colour-tunable hydrogel and deep ultraviolet birefringent modulator [4,5]. Our finding provides an entry point for using wide-bandgap 2D materials as next-generation optical LCs.   References [1] B. Ding, et al, Nat. Commun. 11, 3725 (2020). [2] B. AbstractD: Thin Film Transistors (TFT) are being widely used as backplane to drive large area electronics such as LCD, OLED and micro-LED display, and tactile/pressure sensors. Amorphous-Si, Poly-Si, and oxide semiconductors are commonly used in backplane TFT. High carrier mobility, high on/off ratio and stability are important characteristics for backplane TFT. Two-dimensional semiconductors, especially MoS2, are proposed as an alternative material to improve the mechanical flexibility of the resulting devices. In this talk, we present the fabrication of MoS2-based backplane TFT to drive large area display and tactile sensor. For this purpose, we synthesized high-quality monolayer MoS2 through a modified metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) process and fabricated TFT array using conventional photolithography and etching processes. The good mechanical properties of MoS2 enables the development of various flexible devices that cannot be easily reproduced with conventional materials. Examples of devices include wearable OLED and micro-LED display and wearable tactile sensor.

TitleA: 2D Semiconductor Optoelectronics: Advances, Challenges and Opportunities
AbstractA: In this talk, I will present recent advancements on understanding and controlling the radiative and non-radiative recombination rates in various 2D semiconductor systems. I will discuss the mechanisms by which non-radiative recombination can be fully suppressed in TMDC monolayers, resulting in near-unity photoluminescence quantum yield at room temperature despite the presence of large defect densities.  I will discuss an AC carrier injection mechanism to enable bright light emitting devices using monolayers, overcoming the problem of Schottky contacts. Finally, I will discuss potential applications for black phosphorous (BP) thin films for midwave-IR photo detection and emission. Specifically, the BP based devices are shown to exhibit higher detectivity and luminescence efficiencies over state-of-the-art III-V and II-VI devices in mid-IR, owing to the lower Auger recombination rates and unusually low surface recombination velocity.
TitleD: Graphene-enhanced van der Waals contacts between three-dimentional metals and two-dimentional semiconductors
AbstractD: Atomically thin two-dimensional semiconductors have shown great potentials for ultrashort channel field-effect transistors (FETs) in next-generation electronics. As FETs are scaling down, the device performance is dominated by the contact resistance of the semiconductor/metal interface. The optimization of the electrical contacts is hindered by the intractable surface states and accompanying energy barriers, and it is still challenging to realize ultraclean electrical contacts with low resistances. Here, we demonstrate a reliable graphene-enhanced vdWs assembly strategy for realizing atomically flat, ultraclean and defect-free semiconductor/graphene/metal van der Waals interfaces, in which monolayer graphene serves as a conductive coupling layer between metals and 2D semiconductor for eliminating metal-induced-gap-states in 2D semiconductiors and improving electrical contacts. Through this approach, we realized ohmic contacts for both p- and n-type 2D semiconductors, achieving p-type MoTe2, p-type black phosphorus and n-type MoS2 FETs with an on-state current density of 404, 1520 and 761 μA μm-1, respectively.

TitleA: Van der Waals Heterostructures for Orbital Gating in Photo-transistors and Electronic Spectroscopy
AbstractA:
Each atomic layer in van der Waals heterostructures possesses a distinct electronic band structure that can be manipulated for unique device operations. The subtle but critical band coupling between the atomic layers, varied by the momentum (valley) of electrons and external electric fields in device operation, has not yet been presented or applied to designing original devices with the full potential of van der Waals heterostructures.
In this talk, I will introduce interlayer coupling spectroscopy at the device-scale based on the negligible quantum capacitance of two-dimensional semiconductors in lattice-orientation-tuned, resonant tunneling transistors (Figure below). The effective band structures of the mono-, bi-, and quadrilayer of MoS2 and WSe2, modulated by the orientation- and external electric field-dependent interlayer coupling in device operations, could be demonstrated by the new conceptual spectroscopy overcoming the limitations of the former optical, photoemission, and tunneling spectroscopy. Based on the vertical heterojunction, single-defect resonant transistors, and novel orbital-gating phototransistors could be developed.

AbstractB: In the modern nano-electronics overheating is one of the major reasons for device failure and it can also cause irreversible damage to circuit components. Management of this excess heat is a difficult challenge that has resulted in significant recent research efforts to control and manipulate heat transport, which are key issues for thermal engineering and waste heat conversion. Accordingly, in the advent of 2D material-based electronics, an understanding of their thermal properties in addition to their electric ones is crucial to enable efficient transfer of excess heat away from the electronic components.   In-plane, phonon thermal conductivity (κ) in 2D materials spans over wide range, from very high in graphene (2000 W/mK) and hBN (700-450 W/mK) to below 100 W/mK in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs. For instance, MoS2, one of the most representative TMD exhibits the thickness dependent κ which increases from ~25 W/mK to ~ 100 W/mK with the thickness increasing from single layer to bulk. Therefore, 2D materials offer an interesting platform to study thermal transport in the nanoscale. The current understanding of thermal transport by phonons will be reviewed considering a few exemplary cases.   In this talk I will revise the advances in the field of thermal transport in 2D materials and discuss the novel concepts and recent results in the field. Especially I will focus on controlling of the thermal conductivity of the 2D materials, which can be achieved with various approaches, for example adjusting their geometry, thickness, and the amount of structural defects, such as vacancies or grain boundaries. In van der Waals structures a desired thermal conductivity can be achieved by the proper choice of layers and their relative orientation.
TitleC: Growth of single-crystal van der Waals layered materials
AbstractC: Van der Waals (vdW) layered materials, such as graphene, hexagonal boron nitride, and transition metal dichalcogenides, have gained attention due to their unique physical and chemical properties, including high exciton binding energy and significant magnetic resistance, which enable novel electronic applications. To fully harness these inherent properties for industrial use, large-scale, single-crystal vdW layered materials are essential. In this presentation, we discuss recent advancements in the growth of single-crystal vdW layered materials on atomic sawtooth surfaces at a wafer scale and their device applications.

TitleA: Charge and Energy Transfer Mechanisms in Type-II van der Waals Heterostructures
AbstractA: Van der Waals (vdW) heterojunctions present a fascinating world to explore for photophysics experiments! As layered transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have thickness-dependent characteristics when approaching the monolayer limit, their optical and electronic properties can be tuned almost limitlessly by stacking TMDs in different configurations. Given their excitonic nature, and the dependence of their excitonic properties on the surrounding environment, TMDs can exhibit new phenomena when covered by organic semiconductors. Understanding the competition between charge transfer and energy transfer in vdW heterojunctions, particularly in the presence of organic semiconductors, is important to drive new advances in TMD-based optoelectronic devices. Optical spectroscopy is a very powerful tool to elucidate charge and energy transfer mechanisms in semiconductor heterojunctions. We have previously demonstrated ultrafast charge transfer between CVD-grown MoS2 and conjugated polymers using femtosecond transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy. We showed that MoS2 actively contributes to the charge photogeneration process in heterojunctions with either conjugated polymers, or a polymer:fullerene blend. Additionally, photoluminescence (PL) quenching and time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) measurements can reveal additional information about energy transfer between layers. In this talk, I will discuss our recent findings on photophysical processes within three novel type-II vdW heterostructure systems: 1) ReS2/MoSe2 2D/2D heterostructures; MoS2-WS2 heterostructures doped with benzodithophene (BDT) molecules; and large-area, single-crystal MoS2 interfaced with high-efficiency organic solar active layers (i.e., PM6:Y6). We demonstrated that in ReS2/MoSe2 heterostructures, resonant energy transfer dominates over charge transfer from ReS2 to MoSe2, even without a charge-blocking interlayer. We have shown that the BDT molecule can heal defects within the MoS2-WS2 heterostructure, and I will discuss the impact this has on its photophysics. Finally, I will show that the MoS2 can act as an effective hole transport layer in high-efficiency solar cells by leading to long-lived charges in both the MoS2 and the organic layers. I will discuss on-going and future work in the KAUST Solar Center to incorporate 2D semiconductors into high-efficiency photovoltaics.

TitleC: Epitaxial Growth of 2D MoS2 and WS2 using inorganic molecular precursors, MOCl4 and WOCl4: The critical role of Substrate Surface Termination
AbstractC: Our study demonstrate the exceptional chemical route for synthesizing uniform and large-area films of monolayer MoS2 and WS2, ones of representative transition metal dichalcogenides. The conventional precursors for MoS2 and WS2 synthesis by chemical vapor deposition (CVD), such as solid-state metal oxides or metal-organic molecules causes the several drawbacks, like the deficient reproducibility and the inevitable carbon contaminations. To overcome these limitations, we developed the inorganic molecular CVD method using inorganic molecular precursors, MOCl4 and WOCl4, with gaseous sulfur precursor, H2S, which enables the precise control of the partial pressure for all precursors during CVD process. Consequently, the of high-quality and carbon-free MoS2 and WS2 films can be synthesized only for several tens of minutes. In addition, the epitaxial growth of MoS2 film was successfully demonstrated, which exhibited excellent electrical and optical properties, outstanding homogeneity, and orientation selectivity. The systematic investigation of the effect of growth temperature on the crystallographic orientations of MoS2 revealed that the surface termination of the sapphire substrate depending on the growth temperature, plays a critical role in determining the crystallographic orientation selectivity of MoS2. The elaborate surface characterizations combined with theoretical calculations suggested that the formation of half-Al-terminated surface at a high temperature is crucial for the epitaxial growth of MoS2 on a C-plane sapphire substrate. We believe that the extended knowledges by our work, regarding the roles of the substrate surface termination on the epitaxial growth, will highly contribute to designing the efficient epitaxial growth routes for single crystalline 2D materials.
